newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's banks to rescue ailing Kia Group.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's banks to rescue ailing Kia Group.

text.p: South Korean banks on Tuesday stepped in to rescue the Kia Group, the country's eighth largest business conglomerate whose carmaking flagship has been battered by slumping sales.
Creditors selected 18 of Kia's 38 affiliates for rescue, according to a statement from the Korea First Bank, the group's biggest creditor.
It was the third such rescue by a consortium of banks and financial institutions in three months.

"The creditor's decision was unexpected because we have tried our best to meet our loan payments, but the decision will keep our bank accounts open and there will be no damage to our customers," said Ahn Suk-woo, group spokesman.
He said the rescue plan would be in effect for two months.
The Kia Group had total debts of 9.54 trillion won ($10.7 billion) at the end of May, according to the Korea Federation of Banks.
The Korea First Bank statement blamed the deteriorating business performances of major Kia units for the crisis and said creditors would meet on July 30 to work out details of the package.
IBCA, the European rating agency, said it would review its Korean bank and sovereign ratings after the announcement that the Kia Group was seeking protection for some of its subsidiaries.
IBCA noted it had recently lowered a number of Korean bank ratings but that the problems of Kia would place further pressure on an already over-extended banking system.
Analysts said creditor banks could replace Kia's current management or promote a third-party takeover.
"Creditors must be concerned about their loans to Kia, so they might seek a third party to take over the ailing group," said Sohn Jong-won, analyst at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.

"The government may have to intervene to bail out the Kia Group because the creditors' rescue plan is not going to help improve Kia's management very much," said Yang Dong-ki, analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Like other car manufacturers, Kia has been struggling because of a severe industry downturn. It had sought to stay afloat by cutting jobs and shedding assets.
Kia's woes were compounded by persistent rumours over its financial health that savaged the share prices of its listed affliates, including Kia Motors, one of the country's top three automakers.
A challenge by newcomer Samsung Motors, rumoured to be interested in buying Kia Motors, whose largest single shareholder is U.S. auto giant Ford Motor with 16.9 percent, added to a sense of crisis.

The bail-out reflects concern by authorities to prevent a domino-effect of bankruptcies following the country's biggest ever corporate failure in January when Hanbo Steel collapsed under 6.6 trillion won in debt.
Also included in the bail-out plan are Asia Motors, Kia Steel, Kisan, Kia Precision, Kia Service and 12 other unlisted units.
In the previous two bail-outs of the Jinro and Dainong Groups, the family owners were required to give up management control to creditors in return for funds.
The Korea Stock Exchange halted trading in all six listed Kia shares for the afternoon session. Trading would resume on Wednesday, an exchange official said.
News of the rescue sent share prices tumbling on the exchange. The leading index plunged more than two percent but later recovered to end the day down 1.23 percent, or 9.40 points, to 755.05.

In an interview with Reuters last week, Kia chairman Kim Sun-hong, said he believed the group was on the road to recovery following new harmony between labour and management that had led to agreements on a restructuring.
The group is seeking to cut Kia Motors' 20,000-strong workforce by 10 percent. Asia Motors' union has agreed to a reduction of 1,447 jobs from 9,200.
The group had announced it would sell some 795 billion won worth of idle assets. ($1 = 891 won)
